newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel cuts rates but markets unhappy.
newsitem.headline: Israel cuts rates but markets unhappy.

text.p: The Bank of Israel announced a cut in short-term interest rates of 0.3 percentage point to an annualised 15.2 percent on Monday, but the capital and foreign currency markets responded negatively.

The central bank said it was influenced by mixed indicators. Consumer prices have risen only moderately in the past few months and M1 money supply has expanded at a rate consistent with economic activity.
But inflation is still running above the government's 1996 target of 8-10 percent and inflationary expectations in the capital market have been edging higher.
Israeli banks announced they would cut their prime rates in tandem to 16.7 percent.
The rate cut, which takes effect on Thursday, brings the cumulative reduction to 1.8 percentage points since August. But the markets expressed disappointment with the news.

"People were expecting a cut of 0.5 point or more because everyone was saying that (Bank of Israel Governor Jacob) Frenkel is under political pressure," said Jonathan Katz, senior economist at Capital Holdings consultants.
Trading was volatile in the foreign currency market with the dollar falling to 3.25 shekels from 3.28. The shekel had weakened last week in expectation of a rate cut this week.
Dollar-linked bonds also came under selling pressure.

"In dollar-linked bonds there was a lot of supply this morning because interest rates will not help bring a further depreciation of the shekel," said Gidi Halperin of Meitav Investments and Securities.

The Tel Aviv bourse's benchmark Mishtanim index of the top 100 stocks was off 1.5 percent at 185.20 points. "I don't see a turnaround in the market coming, at least not in the stock market," Halperin said.
Business leaders attacked the central bank, saying restrictive monetary policy would exacerbate the economy's slowdown and hurt exporters by strengthening the shekel.
"The Bank of Israel governor seems to live in a bubble and doesn't see the deepening economic crisis," warned Zvi Amit, director of the Federation of Israeli Chambers of Commerce.
Frenkel has indicated that if the government reduces its budget deficit he can ease montetary policy, but exporters said that would take too long.
"We need monetary steps to lower interest rates and correct the foreign exchange rate without waiting for fiscal steps," said Amir Makov, chairman of the Israel Export Institute.
